newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada and Chile sign free trade agreement.
newsitem.headline: Canada and Chile sign free trade agreement.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and Chilean President Eduardo Frei on Monday signed a free trade accord that is a stepping-stone for Chile to become a member of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

"This agreement demonstrates Canada's determination to create jobs and encourage economic growth through trade liberalisation," Chretien said at the signing ceremony for the accord reached after 11 months of negotiations.

NAFTA groups Canada, the United States and Mexico, and some of the provisions of the agreement between Ottawa and Santiago were modelled on NAFTA clauses. Chretien said he would discuss speeding up Chile's NAFTA membership with U.S. President Bill Clinton when they meet at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Philippines next week.

"We will keep pushing the United States. And my personal view is that the President of the United States, Mr. Clinton, desires very strongly to be able to sign (Chile's membership of NAFTA)," Chretien told reporters.

Talks on Chile's membership of the North American trade bloc have been put on hold because the Clinton administration was unable to obtain "fast-track" negotiating authority from the Republican-led Congress.

Chile has said it will not sit down to negotiate on NAFTA until Washington obtains that authority, which limits the power of Congress to change a proposed trade accord by allowing legislators to either pass or reject the deal.

"It is very important that this agreement that we have with Mexico and the United States be expanded," Chretien said. He said Canada would take advantage of being the first of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations to have a free trade deal with Chile.
"When you are first, you are always in a better position than when you are last," Chretien said.

"We have this situation with Cuba, for example. We're there, the Americans are not there. Eventually they will be there. But at that time they will come in Canadian-owned hotels," he said, alluding to a dispute between Ottawa and Washington over a U.S. law that punishes foreign investors doing business with Cuba.

Canadian officials said the agreement with Chile could double trade between the two countries, which totalled C$666 million ($483 million) in 1995. Chile is now Canada's fourth largest export market in South America, buying C$387 million ($286 million) in Canadian goods and services in 1995.
The free trade pact calls for the immediate removal of tariffs on 75 percent of trade between Chile and Canada, with most other tariffs to be phased out over five years.

Canada is already one of the main investors in Chile, with C$7 billion ($5.2 billion) in actual and planned investment, but Ottawa was unable to get an exemption from a rule that requires foreign investors to deposit 30 percent of their capital with Chile's central bank. Instead, the agreement includes a clause that will automatically grant Canadian investors "the benefits of any future liberalisation."
The pact also includes side agreements on environmental and labour cooperation and provides for the elimination of any anti-dumping duties the two countries might have within a maximum of six years.
